To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

two novel mutations in the fibrinogen gene, p.Gly366‐Ser (fibrinogen Beograd), located in the C‐terminal region of the fibrinogen molecule, and p.Asp316‐Asn (fibrinogene Pisa), located in the γ‐module, have been found to be responsible for FSD.
we identified two novel FGG mutations in patients with FSD and we showed the importance of γ chain mutations in FSD pathogenesis.

we have identified two novel mutations, one of which has been reported for the first time in the literature (p.Gly366Ser), and we have characterized them in the context of the fibrinogen molecule, and we have shown that the two mutations are likely to be pathogenic.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of the genetic cause of FSD in two patients, one of whom is a member of a family with a history of recurrent thrombosis and a history of recurrent miscarriage.
the identification of the genetic defect(s) underlying the FSD of two patients with hypofibrinogenaemia and the characterization of the functional consequences of the novel missense mutations.
the molecular characterization of two novel FSD cases, identified in two unrelated Italian families.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
mutations within the fibril‐forming domains of the fibrinogen molecule (Aα‐Bβ‐γ) cause hypofibrinogemia, whereas mutations within the γ‐module are responsible for FSD.
the fibrinogen gamma chain is involved in the pathogenesis of FSD and that the other chains do not have a role.
FSD is an extremely rare condition, caused by γ‐chain mutations and associated with low fibrinogen levels.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
FSD is a rare disorder caused by γ‐chain mutations that impact on the γ‐module and that it can be associated with a wide clinical variability.
FSD is a rare disorder with a wide spectrum of clinical manifestations and a heterogeneous pathogenic basis.
the fibrinogen gamma chain is the most important chain in fibrinogen assembly.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the fibrinogen gamma‐module is the most vulnerable to mutations, which may explain the high frequency of FGG mutations in fibrinogen deficiency.
fibrinogen γ mutations may also cause FSD, a finding that may impact on the diagnostic workup of patients with hypofibrinogenaemia.
